sections.title: In grep
sections.body: grep uses Basic Regex (BRE) by default. Use grep -E for Extended Regex (ERE), which supports familiar +, ?, |, and grouping (...) without extra backslashes. Use grep -o to print only matched substrings. Prefer single quotes around the pattern so Bash does not expand it.

sections.body: A plain dot in regex matches any single character, so ynetnews.com would also match ynetnewsXcom. Write ynetnews\.com when you need an actual dot. A URL is just text being matched; grep does not open the URL.

sections.title: Variable assignment
sections.body: For a simple assignment, write name=value with NO spaces on either side of =. Spaces split words into separate shell arguments. Do not place $ before the variable name when assigning it.

sections.title: Reading a value
sections.body: Use $name or, more safely inside other text, ${name} to expand an existing variable. Use quotes around expansions to prevent unwanted word splitting and globbing.

sections.title: Not every equals sign is an assignment
sections.body: Inside [[ ... ]], = or == compares strings; inside (( ... )), = can assign arithmetic values. The spaces allowed in these constructs are different from ordinary variable assignments.

sections.title: Keep in mind
sections.body: Variables can store text, including the stdout of a command through $(...). Bash variables cannot hold NUL bytes; command substitution also removes trailing newline characters.

topics.name: quoting
topics.description: Quoting protects text from shell interpretation. Single and double quotes are useful for different reasons.

sections.title: Single quotes
sections.body: 'text' treats nearly everything inside literally. Even $HOME remains the characters $HOME. A single quote cannot be placed directly inside a single-quoted string.

sections.title: Double quotes
sections.body: "text" protects spaces and most shell metacharacters but still permits variable and command substitution, such as "$HOME" and "$(date)".

sections.title: Why quote URLs?
sections.body: An unquoted URL containing &, ?, * or spaces can be split or interpreted by Bash. Quoting URLs prevents these surprises. A simple URL may happen to work unquoted, but quoting is a reliable habit.

sections.title: Regex patterns
sections.body: Use single quotes for static regex patterns such as 'https://example\.com/[0-9]+'. The quotes are for Bash, not for enabling regex in grep.

topics.name: stdin / stdout / stderr
topics.summary: Understand where program input and output go
topics.description: Unix programs commonly use three standard streams: input (stdin), normal output (stdout), and error output (stderr).

sections.title: The three streams
sections.body: They are connections, not Bash variables. By default stdin reads from the terminal, while stdout and stderr are displayed in the terminal. A command may instead read from a file or another process.

Normal output intended for data or results.
Diagnostics, warnings, and error messages.

sections.title: Redirection
sections.body: Use > for stdout to a file, 2> for stderr to a file, and < to read stdin from a file. A pipe connects one process's stdout to another process's stdin.

sections.title: Exit status is separate
sections.body: After a command finishes, Bash receives an exit status. Status 0 typically means success; a nonzero status signals a condition such as an error or no match. Exit status is not the text on stdout.

examples.description: Write hello to stdout.

Use 2> separately when you need error messages.

topics.name: pipes & redirection
topics.description: Bash operators route data between files, variables, and commands. They are shell syntax, not separate executables.

sections.title: Common operators
sections.body: Each operator has a different role:

items.definition: Connect the stdout of the command on the left to the stdin of the command on the right.
Write stdout to a file, overwriting it.
Append stdout to a file.
Write stderr to a file.
Read stdin from a file.
Bash here-string: send a string plus a newline to stdin.
Make stderr go to the same destination as stdout at that point in the command.

sections.title: Passing a variable to grep
sections.body: Writing grep PATTERN page_data means open a FILE named page_data. To search the CONTENTS of the variable, use grep PATTERN <<< "$page_data" instead.

sections.title: Order matters
sections.body: For example, command >out 2>&1 routes both streams to out. Reversing redirections can change their destinations.

topics.summary: Capture command output in a variable
topics.description: Command substitution runs a command and replaces $(...) with its stdout. This differs from simply expanding $variable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The shell executes the command inside $(...), captures stdout as text, removes trailing newlines, and substitutes the result into the surrounding expression.

sections.title: What it does not capture
sections.body: stderr is not captured unless you explicitly redirect it. A program that writes downloaded data only to a file gives you no response body through $(...).

sections.title: wget example
sections.body: wget normally downloads into a file. The argument -O - means 'write downloaded data to stdout'; it is the two-part form of -O-. The -q flag is optional and only controls progress and diagnostics.

sections.title: Memory and size
sections.body: Avoid storing very large downloaded files in a shell variable. A file is often a better choice, especially for binary data.

examples.description: Capture the formatted date.
Capture the HTTP response body rather than the wget progress messages.

practice: Use $(...) instead of legacy backticks for readability.
Quote the URL and the variable expansion.

topics.name: regex + * ?
topics.description: In Extended Regex, quantifiers act on the preceding character, class, or group. Their meaning is different from Bash arithmetic operators.

sections.title: Extended Regex quantifiers
sections.body: The operator affects the PRECEDING element:

items.definition: One or more a characters: a, aa, aaa, etc.
Zero or more a characters: empty text, a, aa, etc.
Zero or one a character.
Between two and four a characters.
One or more digits.
One or more occurrences of the group ab.

sections.title: Bash arithmetic is different
sections.body: Bash's + inside $((...)) means arithmetic addition. += can update a variable in an arithmetic context. This has nothing to do with regex repetition.

sections.title: Use the correct regex flavor
sections.body: Use grep -E for the ERE syntax shown here. Plain grep uses BRE, where + and ? are not special unless the implementation supports extensions or escaping.

practice: Check the regex flavor before assuming a symbol has the same behavior.

nameInfo.text: In extended regex, + means one or more, * zero or more, and ? zero or one.

topics.name: globs vs regex
topics.description: Bash glob patterns and regex both match text, but use different syntax and operate in different places.

sections.title: Bash globs
sections.body: Filename globs are expanded by Bash before running a command. The pattern *.txt matches filenames ending in .txt; the * stands for any sequence of characters.

sections.title: Regex
sections.body: In regex, * repeats the PRECEDING element. The regex .* means any number of arbitrary characters. Unlike a glob, a regex used by grep matches text inside files.

sections.title: Why quoting changes behavior
sections.body: Quoting '*.txt' prevents Bash from expanding the glob, which is correct when you want a program such as find -name to receive the pattern itself.

sections.title: An easy distinction
sections.body: ls *.txt lets Bash expand filenames first. find . -name '*.txt' lets find interpret its own filename pattern. grep -E '\.txt$' searches text for a .txt suffix.

practice: Do not interchange regex and glob syntax; they are different pattern languages.

topics.name: (( ... )) and $(( ... ))
topics.description: Bash has two closely related arithmetic syntaxes, but they serve different purposes. They are different from [[ ... ]] and [ ... ].

sections.title: (( expression ))
sections.body: Evaluates arithmetic as a command: returns exit status 0 if the result is NONZERO, and 1 if zero. Commonly used with if and while. Inside this context, numeric variable names can normally be written without $ or quotes.

sections.title: $(( expression ))
sections.body: Expands to the numerical result as text. Use it inside an assignment or a command argument. This is not itself an if-style test.

sections.title: Logical and comparison operators
sections.body: Arithmetic operators are similar to C:

items.definition: Equal / not equal.
Numeric comparisons.
Logical AND / OR.
Logical NOT.
Numeric update operators.

sections.title: Quotes and dollar signs
sections.body: For a variable that contains a valid integer, (( count == 0 )), (( $count == 0 )) and (( "$count" == 0 )) often have the same result; the first is cleaner and avoids injecting expanded text into arithmetic. This equivalence is not guaranteed for arbitrary strings or unset variables.

sections.title: Important distinction
sections.body: In arithmetic, value 0 is a false result, so (( 0 )) returns status 1; in Bash command conditions, exit status 0 means success. These are not contradictory: (( ... )) converts its numeric result to a command status.

examples.command: count=0; if (( count == 0 )); then echo 'Zero'; fi
examples.description: Compare without $ inside arithmetic.
Calculate a value to store or print.

examples.command: if (( Netanyahu_count == 0 && Gantz_count == 0 )); then echo 'None'; fi

practice: Prefer numeric variable names without $ inside ((...)).
Use $((...)) when you need a numeric value, and ((...)) when you need an arithmetic command.
Always validate arithmetic input when it comes from untrusted text.

topics.name: [[ ... ]] vs [ ... ]
topics.description: Bash supports arithmetic ((...)), extended [[...]], and traditional test/[...] expressions. Know when quotes and numeric operators differ.

sections.title: Three kinds of conditions
sections.body: Use ((...)) for arithmetic. Use [[ ... ]] for Bash string/file checks. Use [ ... ] or test for broadly portable POSIX shell checks.

sections.title: Numeric vs string operators
sections.body: Inside [[ ... ]] or [ ... ], -eq compares integers and == compares strings. Inside (( ... )), == compares numeric values.

items.definition: Numeric equal for test, [ ] and [[ ]].
String equal in [[ ]] and [ ], numeric equal in (( )).
True for an existing regular file.
True for an existing directory.
True for an existing nonempty file.
True for an empty string.

sections.title: Quotes and spaces
sections.body: Use "$name" when passing variables to ordinary commands. In [[ ... ]], unquoted variable expansions are not word-split, but quoting is often clearer. [ ... ] is an ordinary command, so spaces around the brackets and quoted variables matter.

sections.title: Using command status directly
sections.body: if grep -qF 'word' file; then ... uses grep's exit status as the condition. A command succeeds at exit status 0.

examples.description: Print log messages only when the file is nonempty.
Use the portable bracket test.
Prefer arithmetic context for numeric variables.

practice: Always place spaces around [[ ... ]] and [ ... ].
Do not use a bare expanded number as the if command: if "$count" == 0 is not a numeric test.

topics.name: flags, arguments & order
topics.description: Independent short flags can often be reordered or combined, but flags that take values, positional arguments and command-specific order rules need attention.

sections.title: Independent flags
sections.body: For grep, -oE, -Eo, -o -E and -E -o mean the same thing. They enable only-matching output and extended regex.

sections.title: Options with a value
sections.body: wget -O page.html URL means -O takes page.html as its argument. wget -O - URL means the argument is the special value '-' for stdout; -O- is equivalent.

sections.title: Case matters
sections.body: wget -O FILE selects downloaded content output; wget -o FILE selects the log destination. Uppercase and lowercase flags are different.

sections.title: Order is not universal
sections.body: Options can override one another, and many commands have order-dependent expressions or positional parameters (such as find). Never assume every argument can be moved freely.

examples.description: Combined independent flags.
The same flags written separately.

Do not assume that upper/lowercase letters are interchangeable.

topics.name: scripts, comments & execution
topics.description: A Bash script is a text file interpreted by Bash. A shebang controls direct execution, and chmod +x makes the script executable.

sections.title: Shebang
sections.body: #!/bin/bash or #!/usr/bin/env bash is usually the first line. It selects the interpreter when you run the file directly.

sections.title: Comments
sections.body: A # outside quotes starts a comment where Bash recognizes a new word. Inline comments should be separated from code. A # inside quotes is ordinary text.

sections.title: Grant execution permission
sections.body: Run chmod +x ./hw_1.sh in the terminal, not inside your script. Then run ./hw_1.sh. Alternatively, bash hw_1.sh executes it with Bash even without the executable bit.

sections.title: Don't type the prompt
sections.body: The $ often shown at the start of documentation examples is a shell prompt marker, not part of the command.

sections.title: Code style
sections.body: Prefer descriptive variable names, comments that explain *why*, consistent indentation and readable steps. Avoid unnecessary complexity.

examples.description: Common script header (as the first line of a file).

topics.name: line continuation & echo
topics.summary: Wrap long Bash code without adding spaces
topics.description: Break long commands across lines safely and know how indentation interacts with quoted strings.

sections.title: Backslash-newline
sections.body: A backslash immediately followed by a newline continues the same command. There must be no trailing spaces or comments after the backslash.

sections.title: Pipelines
sections.body: A newline after the | operator is allowed because Bash expects another command. Extra backslashes usually are not needed.

sections.title: Inside double quotes
sections.body: Backslash-newline removes the newline but NOT indentation on the next line. That indentation becomes literal spaces inside the string.

sections.title: Split echo arguments
sections.body: Instead of breaking a single quoted string across indented lines, close the quote and pass separate arguments to echo; echo adds one space between arguments.

sections.title: Prefer printf for fixed formats
sections.body: printf uses a format string. It does not automatically insert spaces between arguments and behaves more predictably than echo for unusual input.

sections.title: 80-column style
sections.body: An editor ruler at column 80 is a visual aid, not a Bash syntax requirement. Wrapping lines improves readability.

examples.description: Pipeline split after |; no backslash needed.
Each quoted argument is separate; the indentation is not printed.
Format output explicitly using printf.
Indentation becomes part of the quoted string, producing extra spaces.

practice: Never put whitespace after a line-continuation backslash.
Prefer printf for controlled output.

topics.name: wget logs & HTTP status
topics.description: Use wget -O - to place downloaded HTML on stdout and route diagnostic messages to a log file via stderr redirection.

sections.title: One download, many searches
sections.body: Store one downloaded page in article_data, then run any number of grep searches on that variable using printf '%s\n' "$article_data" | grep ... . This avoids downloading the same article once per searched word.

sections.title: Separate streams
sections.body: wget -nv -O - "$article" 2>> "$log_file" sends HTML to stdout while appending diagnostics (stderr, descriptor 2) to the log. -nv is no-verbose, not no-errors.

sections.title: Choose the log path
sections.body: log_file="$(dirname "$(realpath "$0")")/wget.log" puts the log beside the resolved script path when realpath is available. log_file='./wget.log' is relative to the CURRENT working directory, which can differ.

sections.title: Create vs append
sections.body: 2> FILE overwrites diagnostics, 2>> FILE appends them. : > "$log_file" creates or truncates the log at the start of a run; be careful because it removes old content.

sections.title: Interpret HTTP status
sections.body: HTTP 200 is a success status, not an error. 403, 404 and 429 represent different failures. Redirecting diagnostic output does not prove the request succeeded.

sections.title: Report at the end
sections.body: if [[ -s "$log_file" ]]; then cat "$log_file"; fi displays messages only when the file is nonempty. The log can include successful status lines as well as errors.

sections.title: Check failures
sections.body: Use if article_data=$(wget -nv -O - "$article" 2>> "$log_file"); then ... to decide whether the download succeeded; avoid treating an empty response as a successful page.

practice: Use -nv when you want diagnostic information without constant progress noise.
Keep stdout and stderr separate.
Consider checking wget's exit status rather than just counting matches.

topics.name: pipes vs <<<
topics.summary: Feed data to commands in different ways
topics.description: A pipe connects the stdout of one command to another command's stdin, while a here-string provides a string directly as stdin.

sections.title: Pipe
sections.body: command1 | command2 connects stdout of command1 to stdin of command2. The commands generally run as part of the same pipeline and may run in subshells.

sections.title: Here-string
sections.body: grep PATTERN <<< "$text" passes the expanded text with a newline to stdin without starting echo or printf.

sections.title: Which form to choose?
sections.body: printf '%s\n' "$article_data" | grep PATTERN and grep PATTERN <<< "$article_data" normally search the same text. If you prefer pipes, printf is an excellent choice.

sections.title: Why printf instead of echo?
sections.body: printf has predictable handling of strings, especially those beginning with -n or containing backslashes. echo behavior varies by platform and shell settings.

sections.title: Command substitution
sections.body: $(command) captures stdout from a command. By itself it does not capture stderr. Trailing newlines are removed from the captured value.

sections.title: Loop input
sections.body: A pipeline into while read may execute the loop in a subshell. If you need to retain variables set inside the loop, redirect from a file or use process substitution where appropriate.

practice: Use printf '%s\n' with variables for predictable pipelines.
For line-reading loops, IFS= read -r avoids unwanted whitespace and backslash processing.

topics.name: script paths & variables
topics.summary: Find a script's folder and expand variables safely
topics.description: A script's location can differ from the shell's working directory. Variables and path expansion have different rules in different contexts.

sections.body: In a directly executed script, $0 is the path used to invoke it. Its meaning can change if a file is sourced or executed through a different entry point.

sections.title: dirname and realpath
sections.body: dirname "$(realpath "$0")" obtains the directory containing the resolved script path on systems with GNU realpath.

sections.title: Current directory
sections.body: ./wget.log writes into the process's current working directory, not necessarily beside the script.

sections.title: Assignment spacing
sections.body: Use log_file=value with no spaces surrounding the = sign. Then reference "$log_file" when passing the path to a command or redirection.

sections.title: Quote paths
sections.body: Spaces are allowed in paths. Quoting expansions preserves them as a single argument. The directory must exist and be writable before a log file can be created.

topics.name: VS Code & 80-column style
topics.description: VS Code can show a vertical guide at column 80. Bash shell formatting and Google C/C++ formatting are different concerns.

sections.title: Ruler for all languages
sections.body: In VS Code settings.json, set "editor.rulers": [80] at the top level. This draws a vertical guideline across all languages; it does not reject longer lines.

sections.title: Language-specific formatting
sections.body: For C and C++, configure editor.tabSize: 2, editor.insertSpaces: true and a formatter. In the C/C++ project root, .clang-format can specify BasedOnStyle: Google, ColumnLimit: 80, and IndentWidth: 2.

sections.title: Bash is a separate language
sections.body: Google's C/C++ style rules do not automatically apply to Bash. For Bash, use a shell-specific formatter or keep consistent indentation and wrapping.

sections.title: Helpful comments
sections.body: Doxygen comments describe C/C++ functions; ordinary # comments document Bash scripts. Avoid comments that only repeat what the code obviously says.

topics.name: web scraping with wget & grep
topics.summary: Understand a multi-stage HTML search script
topics.description: Fetch a page, extract article URLs, download each article once, count matched strings, and report results. This example is for text returned by a web server, not browser-rendered content.

sections.title: Fetch the index
sections.body: page_data=$(wget -O - 'https://example.com/') stores the HTML on stdout in a variable. This is not browser-rendered text and may omit dynamically loaded links.

sections.title: Find article URLs
sections.body: grep -oE extracts matching substrings, while sort -u removes duplicates. Dots in regex domains must be escaped with \. to match literal dots.

sections.title: Avoid empty records
sections.body: If all_articles is empty, echo "$all_articles" | while read article can still process an empty line, causing wget to receive an empty URL. Test for empty input or skip empty lines.

sections.title: Download each article once
sections.body: article_data=$(wget -O - "$article") stores the entire response once. Use printf '%s\n' "$article_data" | grep -oF 'NAME' | wc -l for each wanted name.

sections.title: Count occurrences, not matching lines
sections.body: grep -oF emits each substring match on a separate line. wc -l counts them. wc -w counts ALL words in the input; it does not count chosen words. grep -w requires word boundaries.

sections.title: Use status as a test
sections.body: if (( Netanyahu_count == 0 && Gantz_count == 0 )); then ... is an arithmetic test. if "$Netanyahu_count" == 0 is not valid numeric comparison syntax.
